## 1. Architecture and Azure service choices

The API is an ASP.NET Core minimal-API service. On acceptance it writes a durable status row, atomically create-or-returns by idempotency key, enqueues an Azure Service Bus message, and returns 202 with the submission id. A worker consumes messages, processes the document, and writes terminal status. Table Storage stores status and idempotency state; Blob Storage holds the referenced document. A managed identity authenticates all calls. Application Insights provides metrics, tracing, and structured logs. Health checks expose liveness and readiness; Service Bus delivers at-least-once with auto dead-lettering.

## 2. C#/.NET module and API design

Three projects bound the code: a shared domain library (entities, state machine, domain exceptions), the API project, and the worker project. The API exposes POST /submissions and GET /submissions/{id}. The submit handler accepts metadata, a blob reference, and a client idempotency key, then calls an IdempotentSubmitService. The worker registers a Service Bus handler. External dependencies go through interfaces; domain logic lives in the shared library, and projects hold only orchestration.

## 3. Data, identity, and idempotency design

Submission rows are keyed by partition = idempotency key and row = submission id, carrying an ETag, status enum, and processed flag. Create-or-return is atomic: the API inserts and, on a 409 conflict, returns the existing accepted row without re-enqueuing, making retries idempotent and assigning a message sequence number only on first enqueue.

Both services use one system-assigned managed identity with per-resource role assignments. The API needs Service Bus Sender, scoped Table Storage Data Contributor, and scoped Blob Data Reader. The worker needs Service Bus Send, Receive, and Lease, plus Table Storage Data Contributor and Blob Data Reader over the same allowed scope. The blob reference is checked against an allowlist of container names and path prefixes before enqueue; out-of-scope references are rejected at the API.

## 4. Failure handling and operations

The worker claims work via a claim record holding a lease token and expiry. Claim acquisition uses optimistic concurrency so one instance wins; a stale lease is reclaimed after expiry, with backoff and manual review for repeated failures. Legal transitions: Accepted, Enqueued, Processing, then Completed, Failed, or Dead-Lettered, with no backward step except Failed to Processing on retry. The anti-duplicate rule requires confirming prior completion before any external side effect, so redelivery never doubles an effect.

Retries use exponential backoff to a limit, then the bus dead-letters to a dedicated queue. Dead-letter ownership belongs to operations, not the worker. Messages are inspected by error type, retry count, and payload sample via an authorized admin API; replay is manual and tracked, never automatic. Logs carry a correlation ID propagated from the API through the bus to the worker. Health checks probe bus, storage, and blob scope; metrics track enqueue rate, latency, retries, and dead-letter volume.

## 5. Test strategy

Unit tests cover idempotent submit (conflict returns the existing row; first enqueue assigns a sequence), the state machine (rejecting illegal transitions), and lease claim and expiry against in-memory fakes. Integration tests run the API against live or emulator Service Bus and Table Storage, asserting acceptance and exactly-once enqueue. Blob-scope authorization is verified with allowlisted and rejected references. Worker tests use a message fake and assert a single side effect under redelivery. Unit tests run in CI always; integration tests run gated.

## 6. Risks, assumptions, and open decisions

Assumptions: the idempotency key is client-generated and stable; blob references are container and path strings; processing is bounded and failures retryable. Risks: Table Storage write contention on a hot partition, mitigated by spreading partitions. At-least-once delivery makes the anti-duplicate rule essential. Blob authorization depends on the allowlist staying current. Open decisions: Table Storage versus Cosmos DB for stronger consistency; worker runtime (Functions versus App Service); retry limits and dead-letter inspection tooling; and whether correlation IDs survive bus sessions.

**1. Architecture and Azure service choices**

The API is an ASP.NET Core minimal-API service hosted on App Service or a container. On acceptance it writes a durable status row, atomically creates-or-returns based on the idempotency key, then sends an enqueuing message to Azure Service Bus and returns a 202 with the submission id and current status. A separate worker consumes messages, performs document processing, and writes terminal status. Azure Table Storage stores status and idempotency state; Azure Blob Storage holds the referenced document. Azure Managed Identity authenticates every service-to-service call. Application Insights provides metrics, distributed tracing, and structured logs. Health checks expose liveness/readiness for both API and worker. Service Bus provides at-least-once delivery with auto dead-lettering.

**2. C#/.NET module and API design**

Three projects enforce boundaries: a shared domain library (entities, state machine, domain exceptions), an API project, and a worker project. The API exposes POST /submissions (accept) and GET /submissions/{id} (status). The submit handler accepts metadata, a blob reference string, and a client-supplied idempotency key, then delegates to an IdempotentSubmitService. The worker exposes a message handler registered with the Service Bus SDK. All external dependencies go through interfaces (storage, bus, blob) so modules stay testable. Domain logic stays in the shared library; projects contain only orchestration.

**3. Data, identity, and idempotency design**

Submission records live in Table Storage keyed by partition = idempotency key, row = submission id. Each row carries an ETag, a status enum, and a processed-flag. The create-or-return decision is atomic: the API attempts an insert; on a write conflict (409) it returns the existing accepted row without re-enqueuing. This makes retries idempotent and prevents duplicate enqueues. A message sequence number is captured only on first enqueue.

Identity: both API and worker use a single system-assigned managed identity with role assignments scoped to each resource. The API needs Service Bus Sender (to enqueue), Table Storage Data Contributor restricted to the storage account, and Blob Data Reader restricted to the allowed container. The worker needs Service Bus Send/Receive/Lease (to claim and complete), Table Storage Data Contributor for status writes, and Blob Data Reader for the same allowed scope only. The blob reference is authorized against an allowlist of container names and path prefixes before enqueue; references outside scope are rejected at the API.

**4. Failure handling and operations**

The worker claims work via a claim record in Table Storage with a lease token and expiry timestamp. Claim acquisition uses optimistic concurrency (ETag) so only one instance wins; a stale lease is reclaimed after expiry, with a short backoff and manual review for repeated failures. Legal transitions: Accepted -> Enqueued -> Processing -> Completed | Failed | Dead-Lettered; no backward transitions except Failed -> Processing on retry. The anti-duplicate rule: the worker writes a terminal result keyed by idempotency key and only performs external side effects (e.g., third-party calls) after confirming prior completion, so redelivery never doubles an effect.

Transient failures are retried with exponential backoff up to a configured limit; the bus then dead-letters to a dedicated queue. Dead-letter ownership sits with the operations team, not the worker. Messages are inspected (error type, retry count, payload sample) via an authorized admin API; replay is manual and read-only-tracked, never automatic. Structured logs carry a correlation ID propagated from the API through the bus to the worker. Health checks probe bus connectivity, storage, and blob scope. Metrics track enqueue rate, processing latency, retry counts, and dead-letter volume.

**5. Test strategy**

Unit tests cover the idempotent submit logic (conflict returns existing row, first enqueue assigns sequence number), the state machine (illegal transitions rejected), and lease claim/expiry logic against in-memory fakes. Integration tests exercise the API against a live or emulator Service Bus and Table Storage, asserting acceptance, status, and exactly-once enqueue. Blob-scope authorization is verified with allowlisted and rejected references. Worker tests use a message fake and assert single side-effect execution under redelivery. CI runs unit tests always and integration tests in a gated pipeline.

**6. Risks, assumptions, and open decisions**

Assumptions: the idempotency key is client-generated and stable; blob references are strings identifying container and path; processing is bounded and failures are retryable. Risks: Table Storage write contention on a hot partition; mitigated by spreading partitions. At-least-once delivery means the anti-duplicate rule is essential, not optional. Blob authorization depends on the allowlist staying current. Open decisions: Table Storage vs Cosmos DB for stronger consistency; worker runtime (Functions vs App Service); retry limits and DLQ inspection tooling; and whether correlation IDs survive bus sessions.

The worker claims work via a claim record holding a lease token and expiry. Claim acquisition uses optimistic concurrency so one instance wins; a stale lease is reclaimed after expiry, with backoff and manual review for repeated failures.
